name: Wood stove (and wood cookstove)

fuels: coal only where the stove's label lists it
combustion.note: Sealed firebox vented through a listed chimney; leaking pipe joints, a cracked body or an open door spill CO and smoke into the room.

comps.spec: Firebrick lining the firebox: a mid-size Drolet takes 21 bricks 9 in long and 1¼ in thick (229 × 32 mm); a split brick that size weighs about 1.8 kg (4 lb). Good for a rocket stove, forge or oven
comps.loc: Floor and walls of the firebox, held by retainer strips; lift out once the baffle is out

comps.spec: Baffle board across the top of the firebox: vermiculite or aluminosilicate fibre board, about 500 × 320 × 32 mm (20 × 12½ × 1¼ in) on a Drolet, sometimes with a ceramic-fibre blanket on top. Fibre dust is a possible carcinogen: gloves and a fitted respirator
comps.loc: Resting on the secondary air tubes at the top of the firebox

comps.spec: Ceramic door glass, 4 mm (5/32 in) thick on a Drolet, tested to 760 °C (1,400 °F). Drolet says to replace it only with ceramic glass of the same spec, so window glass will not do. Worth keeping whole even off a scrapped stove
comps.loc: In the loading door, held by retainer clips and a flat woven gasket

comps.spec: Connector pipe left on the stove: 150 mm (6 in) on most, 200 mm (8 in) on big ones; black single-wall or double-wall
comps.loc: On the flue collar on top or at the back

comps.spec: Plate-steel body and thin steel side and rear heat shields. Check a shield's gauge before reusing it as a wall shield: Drolet calls for 24 gauge (0.61 mm) or heavier on non-combustible spacers with an air gap
comps.loc: The body; heat shields bolted to the sides and back

comps.spec: Door rope gasket, fibreglass, about 16 mm (⅝ in) on a Drolet Escape 1800, plus a flat glass gasket; replace with rope of the same diameter and density. On an old stove the gasket may be asbestos, as may asbestos paper or millboard round the stove
comps.loc: In the groove round the loading door and round the glass

comps.spec: Optional convection blower: a 120 V crossflow fan about 130 CFM and 56 W, with a speed knob
comps.loc: Under or behind the stove, inside the rear heat shield

comps.spec: Snap-disc switch that turns the blower on when the stove is hot (Drolet F110-20F); Blaze King stoves have a built-in thermostat that sets the air inlet with no power
comps.loc: Clipped to the stove body next to the blower

comps.spec: Catalytic combustor on some stoves: a coated ceramic honeycomb that burns smoke once it reaches 177–316 °C (350–600 °F). Fragile: don't drop or scrape it
comps.loc: Above the fire behind a bypass damper, near the flue outlet

comps.spec: Leg levelling bolts (⅜-16), hinge pins, ¼-20 screws and retainer clips

buildings.loc: Living room or basement; most in rural houses, cottages, cabins and hunt camps
Farmhouse, shop and barn office; old stoves stored in sheds
Stove and pipe display at rural hardware stores
Workshop heater; retired stoves stored at the back
Rental cabins, camp office and warm-up shelters
Scrap-metal pile at depots and scrapyards
Units holding cottage and farm contents
Halls and basements of older rural churches

notes: Read the label on the back first: it gives the clearances to walls, the pipe size and the chimney type, and it overrides the manual (Drolet). With no label it is uncertified and needs 1,200 mm (48 in) from anything that burns at the sides, back and loading side and 1,500 mm (60 in) above (NRCan, quoting the 2001 edition of CSA B365; the 2025 edition revised clearances and is not free to read, so give more room where you can). It is only as safe as its chimney: a leaking pipe joint or a door left open puts CO in the room, and ash holds live embers that stay hot for days and keep making CO (Drolet Part 1). Stoves run from about 73 kg (160 lb) for a small one to 220 kg (484 lb) for a cookstove; lift the bricks and baffle out first, then use a dolly and as many helpers as its weight needs.
